sections.h2: Can a squatter become the owner of a Pennsylvania house?
sections.html:
Yes, but only by meeting a demanding statute over many years and then winning a court judgment. Pennsylvania has no automatic transfer of title to a person who simply lives in or uses a property.

The shorter route is 42 Pa.C.S. 5527.1, which allows title after at least 10 years of actual, continuous, exclusive, visible, notorious, distinct and hostile possession. The longer background rule is in 42 Pa.C.S. 5530(a)(1): an action for possession of real property must be commenced within 21 years, except as section 5527.1 provides.

Section 5527.1 defines the property narrowly. Under subsection (h), the claim covers real estate of no more than one-half acre that meets both of these tests.

  • It is improved by a single-family dwelling that the possessor has occupied for the full 10 years.
  • It appears as a separate lot in a recorded conveyance, subdivision plan or official municipal map or plan.

A possessor may add an abutting contiguous lot that has been regularly used as part of the property, as long as the two together stay within one-half acre and the possessor has held the lot with the same hostile possession for 10 years. The section does not apply to condominiums, cooperatives or planned communities, or to land owned by the United States, the Commonwealth, a local government, an authority or a school district.

sections.h2: Steps a possessor must take in court
sections.html:
The possessor must file a quiet title action and give notice to the record owners, their heirs, successors and assigns. The notice has to use a form approved by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. It must carry the metes and bounds description, the deed reference, the street address, the zip code, the parcel number and a statement of the one-year period to respond.

Owners then have one year to file an ejectment action disputing the claim. If they file, serve it and win, both the 10-year and the 21-year limitation periods are tolled and the court enters judgment for the owners. If nobody files within the year, the court may enter judgment granting title by adverse possession.

sections.h2: Does stepping onto the land stop the clock?
sections.html:
Not by itself. Under 42 Pa.C.S. 5530(b), an owner's entry on the property does not toll the 21-year period unless a possessory action is commenced within one year after the entry. Repeat attempts follow the same rule: an entry and possessory action that ends without recovery does not toll the period for another possessory action unless that other action starts within one year after the first one ends.

A visit to the property, a locked gate or a verbal warning does not protect an owner's title. A filed lawsuit does, and it has to follow the entry quickly. Owners of vacant houses, inherited property and rental units that sit empty should check them on a schedule and write down what they find.

Several clocks run in these cases, and each depends on the route.

Time limits in 42 Pa.C.S. 5527.1 and 5530
RulePeriodWhat it governs
Section 5527.1(a)10 yearsPossession needed to acquire title to qualifying property
Section 5527.1(d)1 yearOwner's window to file ejectment after notice
Section 5530(a)(1)21 yearsTime to commence an action for possession of real property
Section 5530(b)1 year after entryEntry on land tolls the period only if a possessory action follows within a year

If the owners win the ejectment case, any later claim based on adverse possession starts counting no earlier than the date of that judgment.

sections.h2: Liens and mortgages after a judgment
sections.html:
A judgment granting title by adverse possession does not by itself discharge easements, profits, covenants, mortgages, liens, judgments or leases that run with the title. It does not extend or shorten the time in which claims against the property may be asserted, and it does not override the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code or local zoning and land use ordinances.

The remedy is nonexclusive, so a possessor may also have other routes, including a determination of title to a decedent's interest under 20 Pa.C.S. 3546.

sections.h2: How an owner can remove an unwanted occupant
sections.html:
The civil tools are ejectment and, in some situations, a quiet title action. Rule 1051 says an ejectment case follows the ordinary rules for a civil action. Rule 1061(b) lists the purposes of a quiet title action, including compelling an adverse party to commence an ejectment action and obtaining possession of land sold at a judicial or tax sale.

Both the 21-year clock and the 10-year clock run against the owner, so a written notice or an early complaint can matter. Act before a possessor's notice reaches you, and talk to a Pennsylvania real estate attorney as soon as you learn someone is living in a vacant house.

sections.h2: Is entering someone's property a crime?
sections.html:
It can be, depending on how the person got in and what the owner told them. Criminal trespass under 18 Pa.C.S. 3503 has several levels.

  • Entering a building or occupied structure, or surreptitiously remaining in it, knowing you have no license or privilege, is a felony of the third degree.
  • Breaking into a building or occupied structure is a felony of the second degree.
  • A defiant trespasser who ignores notice against trespass commits at least a summary offense, and a misdemeanor of the third degree if the person defies an order to leave that the owner or an authorized person communicated personally.

Defenses exist, including that the building was abandoned and that the actor reasonably believed the owner would have allowed entry. Keep written proof that you own the house and that you told the occupant to leave.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has an occupant
sections.html:
Settle who has the right to be there before you list. A buyer or closing agent reviewing title will ask whether anyone claims an interest, and a pending quiet title or ejectment case can complicate that review.

  • Check the recorded deed and the tax records for your county.
  • Keep dated records of any visits, repairs and tax payments, since the possession tests turn on use over time.
  • Write to the occupant and keep proof of delivery.
  • Ask a Pennsylvania attorney whether ejectment is the right first step.

Once the occupancy question is settled, a buyer can see clearly what is being bought. A cash buyer will still want the same answers, so expect the title company to ask for them.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Pennsylvania?
faqs.a: At least 10 years of qualifying possession for a single-family house on a lot of one-half acre or less. The general limit for an action to recover real property is 21 years.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights to a vacant house?
faqs.a: No automatic rights. A possessor must meet every element of section 5527.1, file a quiet title action and give notice, and a court enters judgment only if owners do not respond within one year.

faqs.q: Can paying property taxes help an adverse possession claim?
faqs.a: Section 5527.1 lists no tax element. Its required elements are actual, continuous, exclusive, visible, notorious, distinct and hostile possession. Ask an attorney how a court would weigh tax payments.

faqs.q: Does the 10-year rule apply to condominiums or government land?
faqs.a: No. Section 5527.1 does not apply to condominiums, cooperatives or planned communities, or to land owned by federal, state or local government bodies.

faqs.q: What if the owner files for ejectment in time?
faqs.a: If the owners file and serve an ejectment action within the one-year notice period and win, the 10-year and 21-year limitation periods are tolled and the court enters judgment in the owners' favor.
